speechtext:
When I heard the minister say that we as parliamentarians and we as Canadians do not understand the native housing programs as we should, it made me sick of heart. I have read the comments of the native people. I listened to the constructive criticism of the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, my colleague from the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) and other members of the House. If that is the minister's attitude with regard to a very serious problem, my best advice to him-and I give it through his parliamentary secretary-is that he read the booklet "Bulletin" which is published by the Canadian Association in Support of the Native Peoples, the August issue. He would indeed be filled in with regard to the serious problems.

The minister should get together with the hon. member for Northwest Territories, the Minister of State in charge of small business (Mr. Marchand), the members of the Indian affairs committee and some housing people from this chamber and travel from one end of the country to the other in order to get a response from the native people with regard to the serious problem that we have.
This motion is timely, and the discussion is urgent in view of the disastrous results of the native housing program and the recent judgment of Mr. Justice O'Driscoll with regard to the Rudnicki affair. I am amazed and appalled at the artificial division that we have with regard to the treatment of native people in Canada. We have a division between the Metis and non-status Indians who come under the control of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. We have the status Indians which come under the control of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand). Finally, there is housing for Eskimo people which is the responsibility of the Territorial Commission of the Northwest Territories. I have never seen such confusion.
We see the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development developing a program for status Indians to be put into position in April, 1977. There are many shortcomings in that program and I certainly wish the minister had been in the House this afternoon to hear about some of those shortcomings as expressed by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent along with others. He is not here, and in one way that is inexcusable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES RESPECTING HOUSING
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell the House that the motion we are studying today was drafted in such a way that we on this side were under the impression that we were considering urban affairs. The hon. member is still referring to matters which come under the responsibility of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. However, the minister will be here at eight o'clock and no doubt he will take the opportunity of entering the debate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES RESPECTING HOUSING
speechtext:
I will accept that interpretation from the parliamentary secretary. I was somewhat confused myself as to what the hon. member for Lambton-Kent was driving at, though I did think he was getting at the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. In any case, I am sorry the minister is not here, because the mover of this motion intended to cover a wide range. What really hurts is that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs has not deemed it necessary to come back and listen to the remarks of the members because the new Minister of State for Urban Affairs has inherited the program to build
50,000	homes for Metis and non-status Indians; as at the end of 1975 roughly 2,700 homes had been built. This disappointing performance is, in my opinion, the result of the artificial division of responsibility and lack of consultation with the persons affected. These people have shown the patience of Job. They deserve better treatment. They have a right to be mad, and a right to demand immediate action.
November 18, 1976

Why are the government's policies inadequate? The main reason is that the housing policies of the government are not based on human need but rather on human greed. Decisions regarding investment capital, interest rates, numbers and types of homes to be built, are based solely on opportunities for profit. We cannot develop a native housing program on the basis of the profit motive.
The private building corporations are not interested in building homes for Indians, for Metis or for Eskimo people. They want profits, as evidenced by their recent exodus to the United States in which country, to date, they have invested $1.5 billion. They have a market place mentality and, this being so, the whole onus for the provision of adequate native housing falls on the government.
Two weeks ago we heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) announce changes in AIB guidelines which affected the valuation of land. This was done to assist developers even though their 1976 profits are excessive. The minister's action is an illustration of government thinking with regard to framing plans to meet the human needs of the native people. This is why Tony Belcourt, the President of the Native Council of Canada, said in 1973, speaking of the tarpaper shacks in which native people live, "They are not safe and they are not healthy: they are bloody time bombs." This is why I believe the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) was attempting to defend the indefensible.
By and large, I am sure the adjectives used by Mr. Belcourt fully described native housing in Canada. If there are certain exceptions in the hon. member's own riding they do not appear to deny the general rule that native housing across Canada is a disgrace and a disaster. This is why the following appears in the August, 1976, issue of Bulletin as the native interpretation of the Habitat Conference held in June in Vancouver:
The Indian people who played their role in the formal conference felt betrayed when Canada refused to accept the United Nations position that profits from the sale of land should not be kept by individuals but should be used for the public good, and when Canada's presentation completely ignored the situation of the native people. But then, those principles-the wholesale and uncaring neglect of Indian people and the selling of our mother earth like a colour TV for profit and greed-are the principles this country is built on, so they shouldn't have been surprised.
That is what the native people felt about Canada's position at Habitat.
What did some of the native leaders say with regard to the native housing program? Bob Douglas, writing in the Ottawa Citizen on August 5, 1976, stated:
Only 2,797 units were built, bought or rehabilitated for the rural and native poor in 1975, the first full year of the program. Native leaders say some of the original goals of the native housing program have been lost. The Native Council of Canada decided last week end to review the program and propose changes to the federal government.
What are the leading native councillors saying? Gloria George, the immediate past president, said there has been insensitivity and lack of interest by the CMHC, ranging from some regional directors up to the corporation head, William Teron. Then she added, according to the report in the Citizen:
Housing
Urban Affairs Minister Barney Danson seems committed to the housing plans even if some of his officials are not.
We know what has happened to the former minister of state for urban affairs. A Native Council paper quoted in the report
says:
The native associations themselves have not consistently supported the concept of maximum client involvement.
This is why it is necessary for the minister to involve not only parliamentarians but the native people themselves.
What is the second reason for the disastrous performance of the program so far? It is the non-involvement of the native majority. On this aspect, Peter Puxley, an expert and excellent adviser on Indian affairs, said he was astonished at the extent of this failure to become involved. He took the view that if control were to be transferred to the hinterlands there was a prior need for the establishment of community development corporations. People would then "learn by doing". Slow initial growth was to be expected, but along with whatever progress was made we could count on the development of new skills and closer unity. It would also be necessary to build an infrastructure. That is why I wish the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development were here today. He is attempting to put in place by April, 1977, a program which lacks the infrastructure necessary to develop the skills needed to carry out the actual building. The necessary corporate forms are lacking, for example, private corporations, non-profit corporations, and co-operative corporations.
The third aspect is the failure of CMHC. The president and its officials are not sensitized to the needs of the native people. When I heard the Minister of State for Urban Affairs speak this afternoon I was convinced that he is not sensitized, either, to the needs of the native people. The results indicate this to be the case. A target of 50,000 units within five years was set. We now hear that 2,700 were completed by the end of 1975-5 per cent-and that by the end of 1976 we might have between
5,000	and 6,000. What an arrogant attitude the minister of state displayed this afternoon when he said that some of us do not understand how the program works. A former president of CMHC, now deputy minister advising the minister, dismissed the very person who could have co-ordinated a program and delivered these houses, namely, Walter Rudnicki.
Let me review the facts, Mr. Speaker. In September, 1973, the Native Council of Canada had an interview with the then minister, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), and pointed out what a serious condition these homes were in. They referred to them as tarpaper shacks which were fire traps and unhealthy, and which could blow up at any time. The minister was shocked and amazed to find that there was no housing program in place and demanded that his officials put a program in place within ten days. He was then advised that there was insufficient time for any input on the part of the native people, which would be necessary to make the program successful. However, since Walter Rudnicki was the chief execu-

November 18, 1976
Housing
tive officer on the planning staff, he and his officials were directed to set up a program.
Mr. Rudnicki set up a program and discussed a draft document with the native leaders. What happened, Mr. Speaker? William Teron fired Walter Rudnicki on the basis that he had disclosed a draft cabinet document to the native people. He was told he was indiscreet and did not show good judgment. Mr. Justice O'Driscoll of the Supreme Court of Ontario completely exonerated Mr. Rudnicki and cast a shadow on the statements made by Mr. Teron before the miscellaneous estimates committee, and cast a shadow on the then minister of state for urban affairs, now the Minister of Justice, in regard to who fired whom. The Minister of Justice said it was Mr. Teron who fired Mr. Rudnicki, but Mr. Rudnicki said that it was the Minister of Justice who fired him. Surely a man with 18 years' experience in government service as knowledgeable as he could have made a great success of such a program.
Before I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to move an amendment to the main motion. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by adding thereto, immediately after the words "totally inadequate", the following words:
"and urges, as a first step in correcting this situation, the immediate reappointment of Mr. Walter Rudnicki as head of the housing program for Metis and Non-Status Indians".
We have removed a person of knowledge and compassion, known for his co-ordination and co-operation with the native people.
What is needed to develop a native housing program? The Indian people have said that we should start afresh, develop a new program and scrap the old program. We must involve the native people-the status Indian, the non-status Indian, the Metis, and the Inuit-in developing such a program. We have to shore up the shortcomings of the native housing bill by getting community development co-operation. We have to set up an administration to develop administrative and technical skills. We have to give sufficient moneys for funding these programs. Foremost, Mr. Speaker, we must settle the aboriginal land claims of our native people.

I should like to thank my colleagues for their co-operation; I will only be two minutes. I was setting forth what was required to put a proper native housing program in place. I said that we should start afresh and involve the Metis and non-status Indians, the status Indians, and Eskimo people in developing the program. We should shore up the native housing legislation which the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development intends to put in place by April, 1977. We should develop the administrative and technical skills of people who are responsible for the program and those who will be involved in the program. We should provide sufficient moneys for funding. I heard the amount of money that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs said was being allocated to native housing, Mr. Speaker, and I say he is taking a peanut approach in regard to launching a substantial and successful program for these people.
We also have to settle the aboriginal land claims of these native people. It is so important to the dignity and well being of these people that the government take the initiative in settling these claims. Some 400,000 acres of land are owned by the native people, and the courts of British Columbia have determined that they do own this land. But no action has been taken by the federal government in regard to settling these claims.

We need men who will ignore personality differences such as exist between Teron and Rudnicki and who will look at the problem of native housing in the same way as Mr. Walter Rudnicki, a man of compassion, a man of knowledge, a man known for his co-operation with the native people. We do not need men like Teron, who are concerned only about land mapping for the developers across the country, and who show little or no concern about native people and their serious housing problem.
I hope Teron will be big enough to ask Walter Rudnicki to return. I hope the Minister of State for Urban Affairs will press Mr. Teron to bring Mr. Rudnicki back and to get him working on this important problem. Then the native people could have some hope, rather than despair. Then they could have some hope that a proper program will be developed, and then they could be proud to call themselves Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in the debate this afternoon. 1 was quite surprised at the interjection of the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Gauthier). He indicated that he did not understand the motion. I do not want to appear to be a nit-picker, but it seems to me that if the motion had been restricted to the rural native housing program, the words "rural native housing program" would have been capitalized. It is as simple as that.
I am disappointed that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) is not in the House, and I feel that the least he could have done would have been to arrange to have his parliamentary secretary in attendance.
I listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson), and listening to him one would think that there is really no problem with respect to native housing. It is quite obvious to me that the hon. member has not travelled very far beyond the boundaries of his own constituency, because if he had travelled in Saskatchewan, in the northern parts of the prairie provinces, or in the Territories, he would certainly have seen the mess native housing is in. For example, I recommend that he travel to the port of Churchill or to The Pas and see the state of native housing in those areas. However, I did not intend to talk about native housing as it relates to the Indian people. My hon. colleagues have covered that subject adequately.
In the short time allotted to me I want to talk about the housing problems of the Inuit people in Canada's north. I read a report in the August issue of Native Housing about the Habitat Conference, which was held earlier this year in Vancouver. At that conference the Inuit people were represented by a man by the name of Jens Lyberth. Mr. Lyberth was born in Greenland and has spent some 30 years with the Inuit people in the north. At the present time Mr. Lyberth is the vice-president of the Baffin Region Inuit Association. At the Habitat Conference Mr. Lyberth had this to say, as reported in the article:
Our people have not been able to influence the formation of policies that affect our communities. In a very real sense, we are becoming strangers in our own land ... In the present situation our Prime Minister and his Cabinet, in dealing with Inuit problems, have been as effective as a kayak without a paddle.
The government is proud of building us houses ... but they simply don't know what they are doing. This system has been built by highly educated, knowledgeable, respected Canadians who do not understand us at all.
That statement is a sad but true commentary on the action of the Canadian government with respect to Inuit housing.
If we read Section 35 of the National Housing Act we see that the CMHC has a certain responsibility. I would like to read Section 35 of the act into the record as follows:
It is the responsibility of the Corporation to cause investigations to be made into housing conditions and the adequacy of existing housing accommodation in Canada or in any part of Canada and to cause steps to be taken for the distribution of information leading to the construction or provision of more adequate and improved housing accommodation and the understanding and adoption of community plans in Canada.
Housing
Notwithstanding the remarks of the former minister on October 1, 1975, to the Northwest Territories Association of Municipalities to the effect that he recognized that there were special problems of construction and design in the north-he indicated that some thought would have to be given to these problems-I am not aware of any program or any study which has been carried out which has resulted in any new or innovative designs for houses for Inuit people, bearing in mind the climatic and cultural conditions of these people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is in the House this evening. It is unfortunate he and his parliamentary secretary were not here during the afternoon to listen to the lively debate which took place on this important subject relating to the native people of our country.
Before I called it six o'clock I mentioned 1 was not aware of any study that had been carried out to determine the needs of the native people, in particular the Inuit people, in respect of housing based on the climatic or cultural conditions which exist. Generally speaking, housing units which have been designed and which are in use in the north have been designed by southerners for use in the south, and in many cases have been pre-fabricated in southern Canada and moved to northern Canada where they are used for homes for the Inuit people.
I should like to quote Mr. Lyberth, whom I quoted earlier this afternoon. When he spoke at the Habitat Conference in Vancouver he had this to say in respect of the Inuit people:
They are living in what we call matchboxes, five-by-twelves and three bedroom plywood houses-thin plywood houses. An old plywood house doesn't keep the heat inside. A new plywood house doesn't either, but at least it's a little better than the old one.
Overcrowding and incorrect insulation cause excessive condensation, which makes the houses deteriorate rapidly in the severe climate. The houses have a life expectancy of five to six years before they have to be replaced ... the houses, in most instances, are too small and fail to take into account the lifestyle of the Inuit, e.g. skinning of animals in many cases has to be done in the living room.
Mr. Speaker, anyone who has travelled in northern Canada and who has visited some of the Inuit communities will certainly verify that statement. Would it not make fiscal sense for the Government of Canada to spend money on research and development in order to design a house which would be suitable to fill the needs of the Inuit people, based on their climatic and cultural needs, and also a house that would have a life expectancy approaching somewhat the life expectancy of the houses we have in southern Canada? I should like to ask

November 18, 1976
Housing
the minister if he would be good enough to tell us what sums the government has spent on research and development for housing for the Inuit people, and whether or not the native people themselves were involved in this research and development. I should like him to tell us whether a suitable design has been developed and, if some research and development have not been carried on, does he intend to take steps to ensure we will get on with the job of researching and developing proper housing and accommodation for the Inuit people?
When speaking this afternoon the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) mentioned the log houses designed for use by some of the native people in the north. I am not suggesting that these log houses would necessarily be suitable for the Inuit people, but certainly I believe a fair amount of money was spent on research and design of these houses. I have seen some of them in Yellowknife, not only houses but other types of buildings. They represent good, substantial construction which would last for many years. This is one important feature of these particular buildings. They would last possibly for a person's lifetime, and when one compares that to the life expectancy of the average house an Inuit person has nowadays, which is six or seven years, then even if the initial cost is high there would be a considerable saving in the long run.
It is interesting to note that the Inuit themselves have formed an organization, the Inuit Non-Profit Housing Corporation, and on their own they have built ten experimental houses in the communities of Frobisher Bay, Cambridge Bay, Rankin Inlet, and Inuvik. Again I would ask the minister if the government is involved in any way in assisting this organization, either financially, with research and development or by other means? The Inuit are a skillful, intelligent, and industrious race of people. Had the government made use of these attributes we would have a different situation in the north today. But what has the government done? Recently it turned over the administration of the housing program in the Northwest Territories to the Northwest Territories Housing Corporation. I would suggest that this is an abdication of the federal government's responsibility. I am not criticizing the corporation; that is a good organization and I do not want to take anything away from it. The responsibility for the housing of native people, which includes the Inuit, is with the federal government, however, specifically the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I would submit that the minister should be dealing directly with the concerned native organizations in so far as research and development are concerned, and with the actual communities and their councils when it comes to the construction of houses. For too long the government has adopted a patronizing attitude toward our native people. Had we adopted an attitude of co-operation many years ago, had we developed self-help programs for them, and had we given them the responsibility of administering their own programs, we would not have the problems we face today.
(Mr. Neil.]
The north is a cruel environment in which to live, and to survive, Mr. Speaker. We have lured the Inuit people away from their traditional way of life whereby they were able to cope and have really offered no alternative; we have offered only inadequate housing and a white culture. Surely we owe it to these people to see, first of all, that they are adequately housed. I would submit it is vitally important that the government take immediate steps to relieve the situation, and I would suggest this can only be done through co-operation with the native people, and through the development of housing programs and designs by spending money on research and development. There must be an adequate and comprehensive program, one that in as short a period as possible will be able to provide them with durable accommodation.
There are only some 18,000 Inuit people in the whole of the north, Mr. Speaker. Compared to the population of the rest of Canada the cost of providing adequate accommodation would be very small in proportion. If the three-quarters of a million dollars that was spent by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in the last three years on government air travel had been used for research and development, it is quite possible that we would have had today an adequately designed house for these people.
I see my time is pretty well up, Mr. Speaker. In closing I would urge the government, through the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, to take immediate steps to resolve the serious problems of housing that exist in northern Canada today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES RESPECTING HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) and some others, I understand, asked this afternoon why I was not in attendance for the debate. Last evening when I read the motion presented by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) I concluded that it did not deal with the Indian housing program which falls under the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development but rather dealt, as the motion says with "urban and rural native housing," which comes under the Department of Urban Affairs.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is only responsible for housing for status Indians-not non-status Indians or Metis or rural people, but only status Indians on or off the reserves. All the other programs, in particular the housing program mentioned in the motion, do not come under this ministry. For that reason I was surprised when I was told late this afternoon that members were dealing with the Indian housing program.
One would think that the opposition, who drafted the motion, would have drafted it to cover exactly what they meant. One can only ask if they cannot draft a simple motion, how can they ever expect to run a government? However, since the opposition has raised questions with respect to the Indian housing program for status Indians, I will deal with some of these matters. But they did not put it in the motion, Mr. Speaker.
November 18, 1976

The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has, as one of its top priorities, the lead responsibility for providing housing to Indian people, that is, status Indians. It flows from the department's general mandate to assist Indians under the Indian Act in achieving self-reliance and in fulfilling their cultural, economic and social aspirations. Housing is an important dimension of these aspirations, not only because it provides shelter and related amenities but it also involves a basic component of the quality of life, of the dignity of both the individual and of the community.
Since 1966 the department has been operating three main programs. The first and largest, known as the Subsidy Housing Program, involves the subsidization of an Indian family for up to $10,000 and the construction or renovation of a house. During the five year period 1970-75, 9,700 new houses were built and 5,500 existing houses on reserves were renovated under the program, with a total contribution of $117.3 million. The current 1976-77 budget is approximately $28.5 million for this type of housing. Today about 65 per cent of the 566 bands have assumed some responsibility for administering their subsidy housing programs. Twenty-nine bands have created band housing authorities to assume full responsibility for housing in their communities.
The second program, which is in addition to subsidization, is assistance in the form of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans which were guaranteed by my predecessors under the On-Reserve Housing Program. During the same five-year period, 1970-75, such loans totalling $10.8 million were provided for the construction of 905 new houses on reserves, of which 305 were provided through individual loans, and 600 new houses were a result of 25 project loans.
Under the third of these programs, the Off-Reserve Housing Program, Indians who are able to give assurance of continuing employment off the reserve can qualify for a repayable first mortgage from CMHC and a forgivable second mortgage from the minister, up to a maximum of $12,000 over ten years. This program also assists those Inuit who have chosen to leave their communities to live in urban centres. Since 1967 some 1,716 Indians and Inuit have received this assistance toward home ownership, primarily in urban centres, through the provision of second mortgage loans in the amount of $13.3 million.
These housing programs have resulted in significant improvements in recent years. I admit what hon. members say about some of the bad projects in years gone by, but since about 1966 there has been great improvement. New factors, such as inflation and the increasing migration to and from reserves, have created new needs. Moreover, acceptable standards of living in our country have also evolved. For these reasons our existing programs are simply not adequate to meet new needs.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!
