speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES RESPECTING HOUSING
speechtext:
Wait until you hear the rest. An estimated
20,000	additional houses, and renovations to some 9,000 existing homes will be required over the next five years.
Recognizing the need for a new approach, last October the then minister of Indian affairs and northern development agreed with the then president of the National Indian Brotherhood to revise jointly the housing program for status Indians. The hon. member for Moose Jaw spoke about a co-operative program. That program was co-operative, agreed to jointly by the National Indian Brotherhood and associations affiliated with it. A joint housing work group was established at the beginning of this year, and new housing policy principles were adopted with a view to considering housing as an integral part of an over-all socio-economic development strategy designed to promote both self-help and maximum Indian participation in administration, design, construction, and management after occupancy.
Further stimulus was provided last year by the United Nations sponsored Habitat conference. Canada was host to the world's first combined government and non-government conference at the ministerial level on the need to develop and adopt national human settlement policies designed to improve the quality of life in urban and rural settings.
In recognition of the acknowledged need for a more effective approach, Indian and government representatives have jointly developed a dynamic housing and community improvement policy for Indians living on reserves. This joint effort is part of the over-all approach to the government-Indian relationship which the department has been developing together with representatives of the Indian peoples through joint decision-making processes in all areas of mutual concern. I think some elements of the background to the development of the new housing policy will be useful to a better understanding of what it seeks to accomplish.
Some years ago the government and the National Indian Brotherhood began to formulate a new Indian reserve housing policy. Initially the two worked separately, and various proposals were exchanged. None met the expectations and requirements of either the government or the National Indian Brotherhood. This led to the agreement last October to examine jointly the issues involved and to develop an approach acceptable to both the Indian people and the government.
After some months of intensive discussions, agreement was reached on seven policy principles. The following is a summary of these principles which were accepted by the executive council of the National Indian Brotherhood, by my predecessor and myself, and which are to serve as a basis upon which Indian band councils can develop and manage programs designed to meet their precise needs.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development will maintain the lead responsibility for Indian housing programs and a suitable mechanism will be established to assure that Indian people are involved at every level of housing policy development and program management. Furthermore, Indian bands will be enabled to administer their own housing programs through band government.

November 18, 1976
Housing
Both housing subsidies and loans will be determined according to the needs and resources of Indian individuals and bands. The methods establishing and applying the necessary regulations, and of controlling failure in loan repayment will be developed jointly by the National Indian Brotherhood and by the department.
The special status of reserve land will not be jeopardized by providing loans for housing to individuals and bands and, as minister, I shall guarantee an appropriate instrument for this purpose.
The housing and physical community development resources of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as well as those of other federal agencies will be made available to Indian bands and Indian individuals who require housing assistance.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to report to you that the mechanism whereby the Indian people are to have direct involvement and input at every level of housing policy development and program management is now in place at the national level. The same mechanism is currently being developed on a pilot basis in Ontario.
The Ontario Indian Housing Council was established through the initiative of the presidents of the four Ontario Indian associations soon after they learned of the joint Indian-government policy approach. Representatives of these associations, together with the Ontario regional office of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, have already been assessing the specific needs of Ontario Indian families and have been making an inventory of local, provincial and federal resources needed to build adequate housing and related facilities.
It is particularly gratifying to note the degree of public support which the Ontario experience has been receiving. For example, the Ontario Society for Professional Engineers has been assisting the Ontario Indian Housing Council on a voluntary basis. At the national level, the National Indian Housing Council is working within the offices of the National Indian Brotherhood on the processes through which a policy, supported by the necessary authorities and funds, can be implemented on an effective and responsible basis. The council is composed of representatives from the NIB and from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. However, we expect other federal departments to participate in the work of the council. The new Indian housing program will involve resources from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Canada Manpower can contribute job training programs to enable the Indian people to take advantage of employment opportunities in the various technical and administrative skills associated with housing and related services. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion is likely to be involved in the creation of jobs and other economic opportunities.
Certainly the primary objective of the new Indian housing policy is to improve materially the appalling conditions under which too many Indian people are still living. Health conditions will be improved. Better housing will also alleviate those factors which make it difficult for Indian children to pursue their studies, thereby enabling them to reach a higher level of
[Mr. Allmand.)
education. Moreover, a decent living environment can reduce the incidence of family breakdown and generally improve relationships within the family. There are, however, other foreseeable benefits which will result from the implementation of the Indian housing program.
One direct economic benefit is the creation of jobs and the possibility of acquiring varied marketable skills. In fact as I have recently pointed out to the new president of the NIB, I view our joint efforts as a self-help venture. We will be relying on Indian participation in administration, design, construction, and management after occupancy. Training and employment will therefore be necessary elements in the program. Another important benefit will be the stimulation of economic development at the band level through the generation of activities related to construction, to building materials, to the manufacturing of house components and to the transportation of goods.
I should point out that, if we are going to involve Indian people in the delivery and management of the various aspects of the program, a major training effort at all levels, local, regional and national, will have to be undertaken. Also, interdepartmental working relationships will have to be developed together will representatives of the Indian people. Federal-provincial consultations will be necessary to ensure the proper co-ordination and planning of support facilities and infrastructures such as water distribution, sewerage, roads and electricity.
This afternoon the hon. member for Lambton-Kent asked several questions about Indian housing. I shall now try to answer them directly. He asked first this question: since the National Indian Brotherhood and the department have reached agreement in principle with respect to reserve housing, when will the minister be prepared to make a formal commitment to the NIB and the status Indians? Mr. Speaker, let me say to the hon. member that on October 13 I wrote a letter to the president of the National Indian Brotherhood committing myself to the program which had been developed jointly, and now we are putting forward for approval that agreement entered into between the department and the NIB.
In his second question the hon. member asked this: will the government raise subsidies for Indian housing on reserves to a level consistent with existing conditions? He says there has been no change in the subsidy in the past Five years. Under the housing proposals agreed to by the NIB and the department I referred to earlier, both housing subsidies and loans will be determined according to the needs and resources of Indian individuals and bands. Under the new policy, they will be increased.
The third question he put was: since the government agreed to establish a mechanism for Indian people to participate in community development on reserves, can the minister indicate what has been done to implement this policy to this point and time? I pointed out in my earlier remarks that the mechanisms had been set up at the national level and that one had been set up in Ontario as well.
November 18, 1976

His fourth question was: would the minister agree that his department should act as the single centre for responsibility and accountability to mobilize funds needed to transfer Indian housing? The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development will maintain the lead responsibility for Indian housing programs and a suitable mechanism will be established to assure that Indian people are involved at every level of housing policy development and program management. I do not know if the hon. member was suggesting that the Minister of Indian Affairs should have responsibility for non-status Indian and Metis housing as well. I am not just sure on that point. However, we will take the lead with regard to status Indians which is the principal responsibility of this ministry.
The fifth question was: is the minister prepared to secure program commitments from key agencies such as Manpower for job opportunity, from DREE, from CMHC, for loan programs for Indians of no-income groups and the need for housing in related programs, and is the government committed to give priority to people in this no-income category? I also mentioned in my remarks that we would do this, that we intended to bring in these different agencies, and we agreed to give priority to those people with levels ranging from no income to $4,000.
Another question put by the hon. member was as follows: projections for 1975 are that half of the Indian population will be living in urban communities; what is the minister doing to assist the needs of Indians migrating to urban areas? I pointed out that the third plank of our housing program in the department is geared to off-reserve Indians.
In conclusion I would like to emphasize that these new approaches still require further discussions and decisions. At this stage, however, the NIB and the department are satisfied that the proposals offer a range of alternatives to bands who may choose those which best suit their own conditions and needs. We are convinced that these alternatives provide more realistic approaches to current economic and social conditions, especially in the light of our experience in Indian housing since 1966. Already more than 50 bands are giving serious consideration to the proposed options. Our hope is that an increasing number will see the solid social and economic benefits of this new Indian housing policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES RESPECTING HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say I was rather pleased to see the minister in the House and entering the debate. I cannot quite understand the idea that had been put forward that a reading of the motion restricted it solely to one particular act under the auspices of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). As has been pointed out, the reference is to native housing; rural and urban were not capitalized as would be required for a specific act.
Listening to the speech of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand), one suspects that perhaps the delay was caused by a need to get together the speech he read to us. I found the most interesting word in it to be the reference to Indian housing as "appalling". Were the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) in his seat, I
Housing
know he would raise a point of order at this spot. This afternoon he would have us believe that that adjective should not be applied to native housing in this country. One always hates to see a member from one's province so flatly contradicted by a minister of the Crown. I would suggest some sort of reconsideration, possibly tomorrow, to straighten that out.
I am pleased to rise on this subject of housing for native people. My constituency has two names, Okanagan and Kootenay. They are both from Indian languages, different languages. The constituency stretches through a good area of British Columbia with several Indian reservations and with acute problems of housing for native peoples.
I have had representatives come to me to discuss their problems in an endeavour to lead anything like a normal, satisfactory civilized life in the face of housing conditions in which they must live. Although they have had my sympathy, I am afraid it has been difficult to advise them as to how best to improve that situation.
It is an irony that we should be debating native housing when the native people of Canada in their own time have made such interesting contributions to housing. One can think of the long houses on the coast of British Columbia with their extraordinary ornamentation, the tepee of the plains with its adaptation to the nomadic life of the people who followed the buffalo, the long houses of the nations of the lands now Ontario and Quebec, or even the kik-willies of the interior of British Columbia, which I would not hold up as an example of great architecture, but nevertheless an interesting example of adapting to a severe climate.
One often hears two suggestions made as to the solution of the problem. The minister mentioned a couple of them. One is that the reservations, at least in my province, constitute themselves into district municipalities and operate in that way. That is easier said than done. In a way it might have something to be said for it. However, one has to remember that municipalities in British Columbia are creations of the province and come under an extraordinary amount of provincial control, whereas the Department of Indian Affairs is a national department in which the federal government has jurisdiction.
At a time when we talk about the possibility of this nation dividing into separate parts I can think of no better reason for holding it together than the fact that the federal jurisdiction is the jurisdiction that has the responsibility for native peoples. While they did not ask to be governed from Ottawa, certainly much less have they ever asked that the nation be broken up or that they be turned over to other governments within the country.
The other suggestion that goes along with that is that the native peoples on the reservations work through CMHC to solve their housing problems. Both of these ideas are very sophisticated.
I would point out that many non-Indian communities wait a long, long time before they incorporate themselves into municipalities. They know there will be problems with that course of action. I would also point out that outside of the individual

November 18, 1976
Housing
application for a CMHC loan, any group of Canadians which becomes involved with CMHC on a group basis is bound to have a very frustrating time. In this connection I recall a representation being made and sent to the former minister of state for urban affairs outlining at length the difficulties which had been encountered in building a non-profit apartment block in Vernon. These people were brought to the very depths of frustration as they endeavoured to work through CMHC.
Many other voluntary service organizations involved in the provision of senior citizens housing have had their plans rejected, rewritten, rejected and rewritten again, to the point at which they were tempted to throw in the towel. We sometimes assume it is a simple matter for native people to endure this type of frustration. But it is asking too much, and unless CMHC changes its ways that institution will not be a vehicle capable of providing native housing.
I am reminded of an experience during my first term in parliament when I was told about the difficulty experienced by a citizen in one of my native communities. Although he was well over 70, he could not get his old age pension because, apparently, he could not prove his age. I went to see my father, who lived in the town in 1912, and asked him how old Alec Jones was. My father had gone there at the age of 17 and recalled that when he first knew Alec Jones he had played baseball with the men. So he must have been already over 70 which, at that time, was the age of eligibility for the old age pension.
After making these inquiries I went to the Indian agent's office in Vernon-that was before it was so lightly closed down-I am not blaming the minister for that, of course; it happened before his time-and asked to see the file of my constituent. It was given to me. I looked through it. I had told my father to be prepared to sign an affidavit if necessary. But looking over the file I discovered the department already had proof of age. It was there on the file.
I took it out and showed it to the Indian agent and said, "You have proof of age. It is right there." He looked it over and realized that this was indeed the case. "Well," he said, "tell Alec Jones to come into the office because he can have his pension at any time". I said "He is not coming in." He asked why. I said, "Alec has been here three times now, and received no satisfaction, and he will not come in again." The Indian agent suddenly remembered he had an appointment the following week in the small town where the man was living and offered to find time to deal with the matter.
I think my story applies to a lot that goes on in connection with Indian housing and administration generally. I am surprised, in a way, that the native people keep talking at all. If the situation were not so desperate, I am sure they would not. They have gone out of their way so many times and received so little.
It seems to me that one of the few occasions on which the native housing program began to get under way was in the early years of the appointment of the late Arthur Laing, the

former member for Vancouver South, to the portfolio of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. When he was appointed to that office I urged the then prime minister, Mr. Pearson, to leave him there because up to that time the position had been a revolving door for ministers breaking into the ministry, and moving on as quickly as possible to something else. I do not know whether Mr. Pearson took my advice, but he did leave Mr. Laing there for some time, and in that year and the following year there was evidence of action in the field of native housing. I wrote to Mr. Laing and told him how pleased I was to see that something was happening. But not much has happened since, and the program which got under way at that time has not been matched since. That was the only time when anything positive seemed to be happening. I suspect that the main reason for the failure since then is that inflation has caught up with the subsidy program; the cost of the houses has multiplied many times and the subsidy has not kept pace.
I might say a word at this point about the government's cheap food policy. I am not suggesting that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) should come into the Chamber to join the other two ministers this evening, but anyone who is concerned about the situation of our native people must be concerned about the very low prices which are obtained by primary food producers compared with what is obtainable by people in virtually every other line of endeavour. Native people are involved to a surprising extent in the production of food on the reservations, many of which are agricultural in character. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) knows what the price of beef is at the present time. He knows that a valuable source of income has largely been denied to the native people in recent years because the price has been allowed to fall so low in pursuit of a national policy which allows cheap imports. This observation applies not only to beef but to a number of other agricultural products.
At one time, the native people used to be able to obtain seasonal employment at harvest time, especially, but this is difficult for them now when the prices obtained by the growers for fruit and vegetables are so low. As we consider the insufficiency of native housing I suggest we should not entirely direct our attention away from these other aspects of native life.
We see a move to urban areas going on. This is a world-wide phenomenon and the native people are affected by it as well. Again, it is often encouraged by government policies.
I am sure every member representing a rural area has had experience with the activities of the Unemployment Insurance Commission cutting an applicant off from benefit and telling him, in effect, to move to a more populated centre. This has been one of the powerful forces working in this country to remove people from a rural setting and forcing them to compete in an urban environment. This is a further factor which should be looked into in conjunction with the motion before us this evening. The division between the status Indian on the one hand and the non-status Indian on the other is one which has been, in a sense, legalized through the Indian Act,
November 18, 1976

forced on the Indian people and not always accepted by them. But it has, nevertheless, led to a convenient situation for the federal authority, inasmuch as it can deal with one side at a time whenever the mood suits it.
We have heard a good deal in this discussion about house design. I am not sure whether the native people are so different from the rest of us in their hopes and aspirations. They too watch television, read newspapers and magazines, and have adapted surprisingly swiftly to many modern innovations, be it the trail bike, the automobile or skidoos. I think some of the things that are wanted in native housing are what we all hope to be able to find in homes of our own. 1 suggest that even the women's liberation movement is not lost on the native peoples and that there are wishes and demands there that are significant and must be met.
I recall the home in which I grew up during the thirties. There was not much difference between native housing and the housing of many of the rest of us in those sad days of the depression. We have heard about the problems of native life in terms of the kind of housing they have. There has also been reference to people skinning animals. My father skinned animals in the kitchen. My mother was never very fond of this, especially if it were weasel or muskrat, because it did cause certain problems. My father was a rather good trapper and he did add to the almost non-existent family income at the time by that ancient and very North American industry on which this nation has been built and based for a long period of time.
I realize that trapping is running into some criticism today and that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) has a private member's bill that would ban the leg-hold trap. I sympathize with him and hope we can find the ingenuity to replace that simple trapping mechanism with something more sophisticated; but until we do, any abrupt banning of that instrument would mean another loss of income to our native peoples. Therefore the urge to find a replacement is a very real one.
Something has happened between the years of the thirties and today in that the gap between the housing of the native peoples and that of the rest of us has widened very sharply. This has had a lot to do with the very slow integration of our native people into our school system and the fact that during the years of the thirties the native peoples had reached a very low ebb indeed. It seemed for a while as if they might almost disappear from the Canadian scene, but they too have been resilient and are now increasing rapidly in number, and a good thing it is too. Nevertheless, we must be prepared to meet the needs of these people and catch up the lost years. The depression years were lost years for us all, but the lost years for the native people were more than that.
We must now challenge the young people. We are educating them and they are moving on to universities. 1 suggest we need more native architects, draftsmen and designers. We need to channel some of the brilliance of design that goes into native art across this country today into the field of architecture. I
Housing
suspect that given a lead they could come up with designs that would relate to their heritage, that would provide the amenities of a civilized life, and by using native materials might find housing methods that would be cheap and effective.
It is a heavy challenge, Mr. Speaker, but I urge the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to take it up and to come up with a policy that will provide native housing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES RESPECTING HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining the debate on the opposition motion before the House which deals with the government's policies with respect to urban and rural native housing, I propose to comment primarily on urban housing. I think it is useful to remember that the rural and native housing program of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is essentially the special application of existing National Housing Act programs in various ways and different combinations to meet the needs of people of low income in rural and remote communities throughout Canada.
The rural and native housing program has three main objectives: first, to provide better housing for rural and native people at prices and monthly payments they can afford; second, to give eligible families and communities the opportunity to become involved in the entire housing process and to create job opportunities in the community; and third, to encourage the development and use of house designs that meet the needs of people in rural Canada and fit their particular lifestyle.
The rural and native housing program, then, was not designed for people living in an urban setting but was created to provide special application of existing programs to people living in rural and remote communities. One might have expected that, generally speaking, native people in urban centres would not require special attention to meet their housing needs as the full range of programs already in place under the National Housing Act was available to them. That is generally true, but it is also true that native families which have migrated to cities often find that the transitional period of adjustment to an entirely new environment creates unforeseen difficulties, and sometimes the problems extend beyond what one might consider to be a short transitional period.
One very useful response to these difficulties has come from non-profit organizations formed by the native people themselves. These groups were originally formed with assistance from CMHC under the non-profit housing program which provides 100 per cent financing to non-profit community organizations for the construction, purchase, or improvement of housing which can be made available to people who need it at modest rents. The program further provides for an outright federal grant of 10 per cent of the capital costs of the project. Some native organizations in various parts of the country have taken advantage of this assistance to establish non-profit housing corporations which buy housing, renovate it, and offer it for rent.

November 18, 1976
Housing
In some cases when groups purchased housing at reasonable prices it was found that the cost of renovation required to bring the house up to a good, acceptable standard tended to push the cost of the unit beyond the budget of those for whom it was intended. The native groups responsible for providing the housing sometimes had little experience or skill in construction, maintenance or property management; but because their courage and enterprise in trying to help themselves in the face of some very difficult problems were clearly deserving of additional support, temporary assistance was provided for experimental and innovative projects out of funds allocated under the National Housing Act for research and demonstration.
Among the groups which have received moneys since 1971 in this way are groups in Winnipeg, Edmonton, Calgary, Toronto and Thunder Bay. In all, about 500 housing units are involved. All these undertakings have involved considerable personal commitment by local native leaders, and they have been invaluable in identifying probems inherent in this kind of enterprise and in finding solutions to those problems.
After March, 1977, assistance for this kind of housing will be provided when necessary under a section of the National Housing Act which enables CMHC, under a federal-provincial agreement, to provide 50 per cent of the funds required to make up the difference between rental revenues and the costs of amortizing and operating a non-profit, low-rental project. Where there is an agreement, the other 50 per cent is contributed by the provincial government involved.
In some cases, of course, especially when the groups have gained more experience, the rental returns from projects operated by the native groups will be enough to cover operating costs, and subsidies will not be required.
Support for projects such as these is not limited simply to loans and grants for construction purposes and subsequent subsidies to cover operational expenses, but financial help is available for the start-up phase as well. Start-up funds of up to $10,000 are available to non-profit community organizations for activities such as developing and incorporating the organization, planning the project itself, consultation with other groups or government agencies, and any other appropriate activity up to the point of a firm loan commitment.
Non-profit housing projects wherever they may be-in rural or urban areas-are also eligible for assistance under RRAP. This means that non-profit housing sponsored by native groups can benefit from loans and grants to restore their housing to acceptable standards of health and safety.
CMHC funds can also be used to provide special assistance, such as training in home improvement skills, so that project managers can do much of the necessary maintenance and renovation work themselves. In addition, CMHC funds can provide the tuition and the incidental costs involved in training programs in the management of social housing, whether this training is provided by an educational institution or by a CMHC sponsored organization. In some cases management

students may be attached to an existing project for a three month period to receive valuable on the job experience.
The social and economic implications of this kind of assistance, which helps people to help themselves, are obvious. As other speakers have pointed out, many native people, of course, prefer to live in rural areas and to earn their living in traditional ways-trapping and so on-but for the native Indians who choose to try city life, whether permanently or temporarily, it is particularly useful to have the kind of supports I have described which ease their adjustment to city life so that they can have a reasonable experience and make an informed decision on whether to choose urban or rural life for themselves and their children.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES RESPECTING HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 know that some hon. members wish to take the floor on a subject that might be extremely important to them. However, I shall make a few short comments about the important subject of housing. As the matter before us today regards particularly native housing I shall make only general comments which apply to every social category in Canada, as some other members will probably speak about social conditions concerning native housing.
Mr. Speaker, what surprises me in the housing area is the tremendous importance of the financial aspect, for native housing as well as for other groups of our society. I have here the monthly catalogue 62-007 giving the statistics of construction costs in October 1976. On page 26 it mentions the cost of housing; it says that from January 1971 to December 1975, the cost of housing money in Canada-the base figure is 100 in 1971-according to Statistics Canada, the cost of housing money in Canada had increased to 130.9 in December 1975. So, in 1971, the cost of money was of 96.5 and the cost of money for housing in December 1975 was of 130.9 which represents an increase of 34.4 per cent in the last five years.
Mr. Speaker, I must add that notwithstanding the motherhood statements made in this House from both sides, the main question that should be raised when we speak about housing for all social groups, for the natives as well as for the French, the English or the immigrants, is the financial aspect.
If we go back to 1968, we find that the interest rate for housing was a bit lower in Canada, that is 7 per cent on the average, while it is now 11.5 per cent, according to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, whereas the effective interest rate, including administrative costs that the borrower must pay regularly above other interest rates, administration costs such as, for example, legal fees, notary fees for a mortgage, then the effective monthly interest rate will be of about 17 per cent, including administration costs.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is not surprising that with such an interest rate Canadians are not very eager to become owners. It is easy to understand why Canadians nowadays would like to become owners but when they realize all the financial obligations that such a move implies, they lose all fancy for buying a home. Indeed, we can still rent a home for
November 18, 1976

$140, $150 or $160 a month, whereas the owner must pay his own way for at least double that amount. Which means that we have penalized, that we are still penalizing the small owner, the person who would like to own a small, one family house.
Mr. Speaker, these considerations bring me to statistics that have literally bowled me over. These are official figures published by the federal government on February 23, 1976. I refer to page 11151. These figures relate to the housing situation in Canada. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) had asked a question relating to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which had made a loan to the Quebec Housing Corporation for the construction of 38 so-called low rental units for the aged. I have here the results of an inquiry into this question, carried out very efficiently on May 18, 1976 by the staff of the parliamentary library and which gives very precise information.
Details of loans by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to Quebec Housing Corporation for residential construction in the municipalities of Saint-Damien and Saint-Vallier in the constituency of Bellechasse.
And I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the figures provided by the Parliament library are the same across Canada because the rates are the same everywhere.
The loan granted to the municipality of Saint-Damien by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation amounts to $537,863 at 103/s per cent interest, repayable in fifty annual payments of $57,617.24. The answer to question No. 3,580 provided by the Hon. Barney Danson does not mention that the interest is calculated semi-annually, so that the actual rate of interest exceeds 103/s per cent and will be about 102/3 per cent (exactly 10.64 per cent). The total amount of interest will be $2,342,999. In other words, the municipality will have to repay $2,880,862-more than 5 times the amount of the loan. Table 1 shows the detail of the loan for the next fifty years.
And we are provided with a very good and clear table and at the bottom of that table we see that after 50 annual payments, the capital being $537,863, the interest is $2,342,999.
Now how can we say in the House that we want to help Canadians become owners of their own homes? How can we seriously try to make the Canadian people believe that the federal government through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is willing to help small owners when we see that in all housing operations all owners have to pay five times their house before they can call it theirs?
Mr. Speaker, I must also say that that upside down financial policy with respect to housing also applies to the Untied States, and since we do not have a Canadian housing policy we must follow the steps of other countries which are often working backwards in the area of housing and others. On page 98 of the financial magazine Business Week of October 20, 1975, one can read, and 1 quote:
Demand exists for rental apartments, but high interest rates push required rentals far beyond what the market will support. Anthony Downs, chairman of Real Estate Research Corp., a First Chicago Corp. subsidiary, feels that it will take rent increases of 20 per cent to 40 per cent to stimulate apartment construction .. .
Housing
Rarely in history has there been such violation of prudent lending principles. REIT expert Kenneth D. Campbell agrees. The banks were shovelling out money as fast as they could-making them as guilty as builders...
The banks are living in a dream world.

And that from a magazine extremely close to the banks, giving us an accurate report on money and saying that those money making institutions are doing so at the expense of housing and the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is inconceivable to think that the federal government is again not using the financial resources available to it because the federal government has full and complete jurisdiction over finance in Canada. Wall Street, New York, Boston or Washington are not responsible for our financial policy in Canada. And yet Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is a Crown institution lending on behalf of the federal government to help housing in general at an interest rate that only a few years ago was referred to as a shylock rate. We now have a Crown corporation which is not helping the people of Canada to become owners, be they natives, French Canadians in Quebec or others in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, as one of the first reforms in housing, I wish that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) would stop looking for ghosts and deal with the problems of finance. We see today under all low cost housing assistance programs an owner paying $125 a month while the federal government must borrow from banks to keep its budget afloat. To subsidize low cost housing the federal government must pay as much as the owner himself to allow him to pay $125, $135 or $140 a month to live in a house he cannot afford when just a few years ago the owner could pay his housing cost himself.
Mr. Speaker, it is scandalous to try to make believe we have a low cost housing policy when we know full well that the owner himself cannot pay. The federal government is paying and through taxation indirectly dipping for the money in the pockets of that same owner. That financial policy is absolute sham. Let us stop dipping in the pockets of the small owner and allow him to meet his obligations himself, and this by reducing the interest rate. I do not understand why a Crown corporation such as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation cannot provide the necessary funds to develop general housing in Canada and meet the needs of the Canadian population and, thus establish an interest rate which should never be over 5 per cent.
When the interest rate will be reduced to 5 per cent, we will be able to set aside all the so-called low-cost housing programs and help those who want to own their houses in the short or long term. The ordinary citizen will then be in a position to buy his own house and to meet his obligations whereas today we are taking all the money out of his pockets because he has to pay income taxes to fatten the finance companies. At the present time, under the excuse of wanting to help the citizens buy low-cost housing, we help the finance companies make millions of dollars, we encourage them, we fatten them. We

November 18, 1976
Housing
want to help the poor and at the same time we fatten the finance companies.
Mr. Speaker, to my mind, we can help the poor without destroying anything. Consequently, we should liberate ourselves from the finance companies in Canada. As far as I know, Canada is a soverign country. Canada has the powers to make laws in the field of finance. The government is not just a municipal council or a town council whose only power is to collect taxes. We have a financial power that no municipality, no provincial government has but we do not use this power.
Mr. Speaker, housing is extremely important both for the individuals and for the country. It is important to make sure that Canadians can afford to pay their own houses without asking for federal help. The federal government has only to leave the responsibility with the poor, the small owners. But, in the field of finance, the federal government should let the poor meet his own obligations instead of taking all the money out of his pockets.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES RESPECTING HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on the motion introduced by my party today regarding urban and rural native housing and to add my commendations to those expressed with respect to the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) who proposed it. It is very topical in view of the present conditions in Canada.
I enter the debate to bring to the attention of the House, the minister and the government, the lack of realization of what one of the programs for rural and native housing can do for Canadians. I refer to the "Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program". The motion before the House reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government's policies with respect to urban and rural native housing are totally inadequate.
In spite of that wording, Mr. Speaker, and with due respect to the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, I would remind hon. members that the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program is a good one. As a matter of fact it is one of the best ever produced in recent years. It can fulfil the needs of the many hundreds of thousands of Canadians who fall into a category where, although they own their own homes, they cannot, because of low income, maintain or improve them. The only problem is that in the three years of the program there has been little or no money to provide the help that the program suggests.
I think it is worth mentioning something that the former minister of urban affairs, now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), said in 1974. He said he was happy to report to the House that we are one of the best housed peoples in the world and that we are also a rich and successful society-which everybody knows. He indicated that in that society, in the rural and isolated areas we have some of the worst housing of any people of the world, much of it inhabited by people of native origin. He said that the proposal the government had made to the native organizations would, in his view, promote

major replacement of that housing but it would require an immense amount of work by the federal and provincial governments and the native organizations. He added that he hoped all three groups were ready to begin implementing the proposals immediately.
To implement programs and proposals requires money, Mr. Speaker. Since the program was introduced in 1973, my province received $600,000 last year and $700,000 this year.
The RRAP program came into effect in 1973 with the following criteria: those citizens earning an income of $6,000 or less could apply for a loan of up to $5,000 either under private home ownership or as a landlord, and could receive a grant of $2,500 to provide insulation, adequate heating or electrical maintenance, to improve appearance on the condition that the improvements would remain sound for another 15 years.
Since the little money invested in the program would be of such help to Canadians, this year the minister decided to increase the loans to $10,000, with a forgiveness factor of $3,750. This change, announced by the former minister, now the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), was even better and more commendable because the increase in the loans and grants neutralized the inflation factors that affected the increase in the cost of materials required to carry out the repairs.
The government even went so far as to prepare, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a fancy pamphlet requesting and even begging Canadians to apply for such loans and grants. The pamphlet is called, "Fix up your home with federal government money" and has a fancy caption which says, "Here's how to go about getting a free grant and/or low interest loan". Let me review this beautiful yellow pamphlet, Mr. Speaker. It is even more beautiful than the one produced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), the "Fix it kit". The back page asks the following questions:
How would you like to get some of those major repairs done on your house straight away?
Maybe you can with some financial help from the federal government. And it may not cost you a penny!
Fixing up your house is more than just making it look nice. Depending on what kind of repairs are done, your family will be more comfortable, their health will be protected, the children will play more safely and everyday living will become more convenient, more pleasant. On top of all this, you will be protecting your investment in your property... at little or no cost to yourself. This is too good an opportunity to let slip by, so find out all about this home repair program and what it can do for you.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, all we received in three years in Newfoundland was a little over $1 million, and many hundreds of people on low incomes cannot afford to carry out repairs.
The political gimmickry continues in the pamphlet when they describe some of the repairs the money can be used for. They list many features: repairs to walls and roof; provide storm windows and/or screens; siding, stairs and steps; fences and walkways; plumbing; insulation; heating system; wall finishes inside and out; floor joists; electrical wiring; founda-
November 18, 1976

tion and basement, and floor finish. They offer these wonderful things, Mr. Speaker, but where is the money?
Let us review more of the wonderful advantages of this RRAP program. Another section reads:
It's true. Up to $10,000 for home repairs.
The government wants to help you repair your house and will advance you up to $10,000 if there's that much work to be done. Up to $3,750 can be yours free. The balance can be a low-interest loan.
Later it reads:
We'll split the repair costs with you.
The purpose of this federal government repair program is to make sure that your home, given normal care and maintenance, will remain in sound condition for at least another 15 years.
And later, it goes on:
Total repair costs will be split between the government and you. Our part is a grant. Your part can be a low-interest loan.
The pamphlet goes on to say that if the grant of $3,750 covers the total cost of repairs, the owner will not have to pay anything back. In other words, if the need for financial assistance is within the $3,750 grant figure, then you get the repairs free. That is wonderful. Even if the amount required is beyond the grant figure you are given the advantage of adjusting payments to family income-to subtract $300 for each dependent child, as well as family allowance, and another $1,000 for both parents.
Let us look at the grants, Mr. Speaker. In this regard we should accept the scale that is reasonable. As I indicated earlier, they apply to minimum benefits to those earning $6,000 or less who qualify for the maximum which is reduced by $750 for each $1,000 over $6,000 until the earned income reaches $ 11,000. Even if you earn over the $ 11,000 income you can borrow at the basic RRAP rate adjusted at 8 per cent.
The program also applies to landlords where, regardless of their income, they can qualify to bring inadequate apartments up to reasonable standards. The pamphlet suggests that tenants bring the program to the attention of their landlords.
I remind hon. members of the detail of the program because I feel, as a result of the needs in my province, that this RRAP program would be of great benefit to it. But I must ask what has happened since it was initiated, Mr. Speaker? Not too much, as far as Newfoundland is concerned. In 1974-75 a mere $600,000 was allocated, and in this year 1976-77 another $700,000-just enough to tease the province into entering into an agreement to extract as much money as possible to fulfil the needs of a portion of its citizens.
Let us look at the facts relating to my own province. First of all what is not said or related in this fancy pamphlet is what are the qualifying conditions which apply to provinces. And what is typical of this federal government's huckster-like tactics is that the areas in Canada which qualify under RRAP have to be designated by the province. One of the bugbears over the years since the program was implemented has been the fact that these moneys are restricted. I have the figures before me, Mr. Speaker. In 1974-75 for all Canada over $1.5
Housing
million was allocated. In 1975-76 the size of this item was multiplied by 12 but it is still not enough.
Let me emphasize another factor showing this government's lack of common sense. The federal government keeps preaching and spending millions of dollars on conservation of energy. It pleads with us to conserve oil, but it will not invest enough funds in order to assist the many thousands of Canadians who can use the help and who, by carrying out repairs to their own homes, could save themselves millions of dollars in heating oil costs. The fact is, it is becoming more expensive to heat a home and pretty soon it will be beyond the capability of the low income earner. In the three years since the program was begun, $13.6 million has been allocated for RRAP.
Let us look at the relief which could be given to many thousands of our low income citizens, Mr. Speaker. In Canada there are one million homes which were built before 1920, and another million built between 1921 and 1945, which means that there are over two million homes between 30 and 50 years old. One can just imagine how many of these need repair, how many of them are not properly insulated and what great quantities of oil are wasted, even though the government preaches conservation. Many of these older homes are privately owned by low income Canadians.
Let us look further at the facts. Statistics for Canada indicate that 898,000 Canadians earn under $3,000 a year, 729,000 between $3,000 and $5,000 a year, and 830,000 between $5,000 and $7,000 a year. How can such people afford to maintain their homes if they cannot even get enough to eat from the incomes they earn? How can they afford to do those repairs which will conserve energy?
There are more statistics available from that front page attention-getter, Statistics Canada. Figures relating to occupied dwellings in 1971 show that over one million homes were heated by space heaters or some such method of heating. How can people who can only afford such heating take advantage of the words in the fancy RRAP pamphlet I mentioned previously? Mr. Speaker, in the province of Newfoundland alone 55,000 homes unfortunately fall into this category. In rural Newfoundland some 33,000 homes fall in this category. They are using heating equipment which is not satisfactory.
According to another statistic, Mr. Speaker, in our great and prosperous nation where everyone deserves a decent home, almost a quarter of a million homes have no installed bath or shower and another quarter of a million are without any running water at all. In the province of Newfoundland I am sorry to relate almost 30 per cent of homes fall into this category. A study prepared by the province of Newfoundland indicates that although the majority of Newfoundlanders in small, rural communities own their own homes, many of these are old homes built in accordance with the standards of the time. A great number of these homes are 30 years old, and even 50 years old and more. They were built without many of the facilities which today are taken for granted. For example, a high percentage of these homes are without water piped inside, inside toilets, baths or showers, central heating and, indeed, either without insulation or with very little.

November 18, 1976
Housing
The provincial planning task forte on housing in Newfoundland notes that with respect to facilities the housing stock of the province lags well behind that of the other provinces of Atlantic Canada, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island. Many of these homes today are owned by low income and welfare families who do not have the financial resources needed to make these kinds of improvements and generally upgrade their homes to minimum standards of health, safety and comfort. They cannot do what the fancy pamphlet to which I earlier referred tells Canadians to do.
The Newfoundland and Labrador Housing Corporation and the department of social services have for the past several months been working together to investigate the housing problems of welfare recipients, with the intent of recommending new policies and programs to improve the generally poor and substandard housing conditions that a large percentage of welfare families are presently experiencing. The first phase of this joint effort revolved around planning with respect to a proposal to place a number of mobile type housing units for welfare families in small communities throughout the province.
A pilot survey of the housing conditions of a select group of welfare recipients, the severely physically and mentally incapacitated living in small rural communities, who would be in receipt of social assistance indefinitely, was undertaken. The result of this investigation was most revealing. Of the 101 families on which information was gathered, it was found that 69 families are presently living in their own homes, while only 32 families are renting. These families were located in most every region of the province and in communities as small as 78 people, and with one or two exceptions, no larger than 1,000 people. The condition of the houses these families are living in is unquestionably poor and in many cases substandard. Most of the houses are fairly old and far from wind and waterproof. Many of the complaints concerned leaking roofs, no insulation, rotting and poor fitting window boxes and doors, rotting clapboard, sagging and uneven floors, and cracking and rotting foundations. In a number of cases it was reported that in winter time ice forms on the inside walls and floors and that furniture and bedding are being ruined by rain and dampness. Twenty of the 101 families have no toilet facilities of any kind, and 44 families have no running water. Mr. Speaker, this is but one small example. You can multiply it thousands of times across this great country. I therefore wish to point out, what a grant of $3,750 under RRAP could do for those citizens.
I emphasize my next point. Since these people must rely on the government to provide them with oil for heating their homes, how can they conserve oil when they do not have enough money to buy food to eat, let alone enough to make their homes reasonably adequate? They do not have the ability to upgrade their homes so that they meet conditions which are appropriate for all Canadians. It must be a source of wonder to many why the government's lack of common sense and hypocritical reasoning would allow these situations to continue.
In this connection I think it worth while pointing out that provincial and federal governments provide on a 50-50 basis

the cost of housing or rental accommodation for welfare recipients; yet these governments are willing to turn a blind eye to conditions in which such welfare recipients must live and allow them to live in substandard homes when, with the provision of a RRAP grant, they could invest in the repairs allowed under the program and thus save millions of dollars over the long term. It must be obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the governments are being penny wise and pound foolish.
Even though some might argue about the need to restrain spending, it must be evident that a reasonable investment in the repair of homes for rural and native peoples would in the long run realize a saving in government spending. Surely hon. members realize that if we provide for repairs to hundreds of thousands of our home occupiers who require such repairs we should relieve substantially the demand for housing, housing which we are evidently having difficulty providing under present circumstances. In the three years since the RRAP program was initiated for rural and native housing all we have seen across Canada is a band-aid stop-gap approach which satisfies but few of our needy citizens.
Let me return to the provincial department of social services. That department currently provides a home repair program for welfare recipients owning their own homes. The program is limited to making houses wind and watertight only. A total of $2,400 may be spent in any one year on one house without Treasury Board approval. For the fiscal year 1973-74, a total of $914,507 was spent on home repairs by the department, yet the federal government only contributes $600,000 or $700,000 a year to its home repair program. The need for a home repair program is evident when it is realized that the province of Newfoundland claims more dollars under the Canada Assistance Plan for house repairs than all other provinces combined. May I refer also to the fact that in the province of Newfoundland a good many of our native peoples are war veterans. I would like to refer to that for a moment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just heard one of the best speeches made today. I congratulate the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for really sticking to the subject and bringing up something which is close to my heart and close to many people who are interested in saves. This country has to realize that a save actually is a start.
With rehab housing such as he has been talking about, and he has been talking about the RRAP program, I have to admit with him that definitely we have a good program, a darn good
November 18, 1976

program, one which we must admit has only been recently put on the market. As for rural and native RRAP, 1 must admit we have only two years experience. We evidently have had problems of delivery.
The program centres around a delivery system which is basically a federal-municipal oriented system. We have had some delivery problems with the RRAP program. We now realize that with the structures in place, the municipalities are more and more able to deliver this program and, of course, to cope with the existing needs which call for special attention.
I want to thank the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe for bringing this up in this debate. I thank him also for his support. He knows at this time we are looking for more funds. The program we had in 1975 was budgeted at $12 million. We are hoping for a 50 per cent increase next year. With his support, I hope we will get it.
Although I would love to speak more on this RRAP program 1 must address myself to some of the comments made in the House today. 1 will deal briefly with the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert). 1 must say that I am speaking personally and in no way making a statement for the government.
The question raised by the hon. member in his amendment is a touchy one. It raises an issue which 1 am totally incompetent to deal with, except to tell him that in my view it is strictly within the authority of CMHC management to decide or not to decide to rehire Mr. Rudnicki. The minister has no authority to hire or fire. We should be very careful about interfering with employer-employee relations. We should also be very careful about entertaining any move that would usurp the prerogative of management.
Even if it were within the minister's authority, I am sure he would not use it because there is a long standing tradition that the management of corporations is the responsibility of the administrators.
The record of CMHC in the matter of rural and native housing indicates that this rural and native housing program has been successfully implemented. The hon. member talked about 3,000 starts in 1975, 6,000 starts in 1976, and 9,000 projected for next year. That in itself is progress.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES RESPECTING HOUSING
speechtext:
I am giving you the story from this end. These consultations are very important. The meetings that are taking place are productive. We have to recognize the reluctance of native people to accept the conditions of existing NHA programs, conditions that other low income groups accept and benefit from. We have to accept that with some of these programs the delivery system or make-up is not properly understood. However, I am confident that it is through this continual consultation process that we will succeed within our present NHA programs to build and rehabilitate housing for rural Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to deal with another aspect of the rural and native housing program that is certainly less publicized, and maybe not as well understood either. The rural and native housing program is primarily a means of providing decent housing, but is also much more than that.
If our only concern was to produce housing, I dare say I would have much more impressive figures to refer to now. We know how to go about building houses in this country, we consistently over shoot the objectives proposed by the Economic Council of Canada and other groups. If our only objective was to produce housing, we could very rapidly use prefabricated bungalows in every rural area of Canada.
But, Mr. Speaker, such is not the problem, and such is not our responsibility. If that were our perception of our role, I believe I would be now rising in another kind of debate. We would be accused, and rightly so, of being colonialists and paternalists, of treating native people as children, and ignoring their cultural traditions. Such are exactly the errors we have been trying to avoid, and quite frankly at the expense of making our task much more difficult and time-consuming.

November 18, 1976
Housing
Because we have been trying to administer the program within the context of total respect for the dignity and self-confidence of the people involved. The thrust of the program indeed is not only to provide housing. It aims at reaching much vaster socio-economic aims.
In that respect, Mr. Speaker, I believe I can say that the rural and native housing program is one of the most promising and innovative, allowing as it does communities to help themselves develop. It is impossible to find anything similar anywhere in the world today.
It has been developed over several years, in close co-operation with the people concerned, especially the native people who, for a number of reasons, are removed from the main sources of social and economic life in Canada.
The final product may be a house, but the process starts long before its final realization. In many cases, before the program can be launched, we must start by helping to organize, promote and even support an association within a community, so that it will assume the responsibility for assessing and solving its own housing problems. From then on, the people of such a community are involved as directly as possible in the decision-making process as to the number of houses needed, the number of houses to be repaired, the families which will get them first and the houses which should be repaired first.
One of the basic principles of the program is to involve as much as possible the rural population in the construction of their own houses and have them devote their energies and their time to such projects. If they do not have the necessary skills or know-how, we try as much as possible to give them the necessary training. This training is not restricted to the construction trades. They are taught to acquire leadership, to show others to help themselves, to develop plans and to manage their own programs.
Many of them often leave a substandard home to move into a well-appointed house. They get instruction and advice, if necessary, on the way to run a house. Some pay a rent or make monthly payments for the first time in their life.
We can help them manage their funds. Finally, Mr. Speaker, we have a family which lives in a decent home, probably for the first time. These people have now the opportunity to develop and live in good health. Children find a comfortable environment to read, play and do their school work. There is enough room to ensure a certain privacy and preserve personal dignity. And I would even say, Mr. Speaker, that those are housing units that the people like, which meet their needs, their expectations and cultural traditions. It is not often a bungalow as we see them in our suburbs. As a matter of fact, a large number of log cabins have been built under this program but they are houses which meet the minimum safety and health standards and often exceed them.
In places where the rural and native people program is working well, Mr. Speaker, much more is to be said. A collectivity after organizing itself to meet its housing needs, can concern itself with some other needs. Having learned to work together, those people can take care of other things, for

instance establish medical services, build a skating rink or a recreation centre, a library, organize spare-time activities, or whatever services the community may need, according to its own decisions.
The support and financial assistance we will grant under this program also helps create a population of highly skilled young people, for instance in the fields of administration and planning. Those people who have already learned a trade when working on their own houses discover that they have other skills which they can use, other means of earning their living in addition to fishing, trapping and timber cutting.
Throughout the country, Mr. Speaker, at the national, provincial and municipal levels, well organized native associations grouped under the direction of a well informed leader have come to light during the last decade. Most of these groups first paid particular attention to housing problems and were sponsored and encouraged through a federal financial assistance scheme available to them under the National Housing Act.
I could say, Mr. Speaker, that the result obtained by the rural and native housing program is clear: some 10,000 units have been built. I would add that it is an extremely fine achievement. If I added that our specific aim was to build 50,000 units, it would also be true and 1 am confident that we will reach it.
However I would like all Canadians to understand that the long term advantages of the program cannot be viewed only in the light of the number of units built.
We will reach the figures stated, but we will do much more. By purchasing, building and repairing 50,000 units, we will help rehabilitate an entire population, most of whom the descendants of the first dwellers in our country. We will help them find satisfactory housing and also regain a new feeling of self-confidence, new pride, new skills which will enable them to meet the needs of their family, to thrive and attain their aims.
When I say that we will reach such ambitious goals, Mr. Speaker, I am not referring merely to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the federal government. We will not be able to achieve these goals without the co-operation and the involvement of other levels of government, provincial as well as regional. However, what is more important, what is absolutely critical is the fact that the involvement of rural and native people, individually and collectively through provincial and national associations, help us attain these objectives.
A program whose success depends on so many persons and institutions is bound to come up against difficulties likely to delay our activities. It is to be expected, Mr. Speaker. But on the whole, I believe we have not had to face too many quarrels and squabbles. This is a testing period as far as this program is concerned, and misunderstandings may occur.

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REDUCTION IN PENSION OF CONSTABLE HALE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RECTIFY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 9 and again on November 16 I raised the question of the injustice done by the Canadian Pension Commission in cutting back the disability pension of ex-RCMP Constable Eugene Hale. Hale is not only disabled by multiple sclerosis but suffers frustration and worry over finances because he is trapped in the web of bureaucratic regulations-that section, sub-section, sub-sub-section syndrome of bureaucracy and legal gobbledygook. These regulations lack logic, common sense, and are unjust and cruel. Furthermore, they are wasteful not only of the few last moments of joy in the limited life of Eugene Hale but also of taxpayers' dollars.
On November 3 Hale was receiving full disability pension because he was in a hospital bed. The next day, because he changed beds-went into home care-his pension was cut by 80 per cent. He moved out of Vancouver's Shaughnessy Hospital to live out his last days of life surrounded by family and friends in Rossburn, Manitoba; his wife, Nadya, a practical nurse, caring for him, saving tens of thousands of dollars in hospital costs.
Eugene Hale is no less disabled today, nor on November 4, than he was on November 3. Hale served on the force from November 27, 1951, until invalided on February 22, 1962. He was discharged from the service as medically unsuitable and given a small service pension, a 20 per cent disability pension, and an attendance allowance.
Although multiple sclerosis is a disease of unknown cause, there is speculation that Hale's service in the north might have contributed to it. It is known that it strikes young people and that it is fatal. Thus young families are ensnared in the tragedy of this disease along with the stricken parent and spouse. At least four RCMP officers-young men-are disabled by it now and are known to be travelling along the same twisting bureaucratic road Hale has gone.
Another western case is that of Garth Hope, Westbank, B.C., father of a young family. I do not know the case well but I hope that the solution in the Hale case will prevent him and others from suffering the insensitive regulations that the Hales have endured.
The confusions are innumerable and could be simplified if the layers of lawyers in each government department were not busy justifying their existence in the backrooms of parliament. Is is as though the taxpayer and citizen is only living to support the legal structure and legal hierarchy of Canada.
Adjournment Debate
In the case of Eugene Hale the situation is ludicrous. On July 25, 1975, Harry Kryhul, a Vancouver RCMP staff relations representative, informed me of the tragic story of Eugene Hale. That was the first I had heard of it. Then, as now, Hale was totally bedridden, requiring tubes to support his body waste functions. The pension board rated this at only 20 per cent disability. Is that not remarkable, Mr. Speaker?
As soon as I received the letter, I contacted the former solicitor general and the Leader of the Government in the Senate, Senator Ray Perrault, who has been my mentor and who for years fought to correct injustice. As a result, on January 30, 1976, good news arrived. The disability status of Eugene was reclassified from 20 per cent to 100 per cent, retroactive to April 1, 1969. A cheque for $22,844 covered the six year retroactive period. It was joyful news. Hale could die in peace knowing he left a nest egg to his devoted Nadya, so that they could build a home. In fact they did start to build a home. Also his disability pension was adjusted from 20 per cent to 100 per cent that is, from $115 a month to $575. This meant that Nadya could stop work to care for her husband at home. As of November 3 his pension was raised to $640 a month.
On November 4 the Hales went home to Rossburn. The joy of reunion with the family and friends was marred, though, by worry about finances. The pension was cut back to 20 per cent, or $125 a month. Pension board chairman, A. O. Solomon, will tell us that Hale can appeal the decision, but why should the Hales be put through added stress and worry in a new fight for the 100 per cent pension that obviously his condition commanded as of November 3, or on January 30 when he was classified as 100 per cent disabled? Why should the taxpayers be forced to pay the unnecessary $36,000 a year hospital costs?
Corporal J. F. Hardy, staff relations officer, wrote on Hale's behalf: "Where is the sense in reducing the pension if Hale leaves the hospital, in view of the obvious saving in hospital care costs?" I ask that question too, Mr. Speaker. Does the minister or the pension board consider that they are serving Eugene Hale and the best interests of the Canadian taxpayers by keeping him in hospital at the rate of $3,000 a month, based on an estimate of $100 a day B. C. hospital rates? Will the minister move to change regulations so that Eugene Hale and other RCMP officers in like position will never again be further harmed by the pain of injustice on top of their suffering with multiple sclerosis? They have served our country and they deserve much, much more.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REDUCTION IN PENSION OF CONSTABLE HALE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RECTIFY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was in the House when the hon. member raised the question and the minister answered the other day. I agree that this is a most important but unfortunate case to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) has just referred, one that presents a number of difficulties. There are as the circumstances which I will describe will indicate, several ministers responsible for the determination of benefits payable to Mr. Hale under the RCMP Superannuation Act.

November 18, 1976
Adjournment Debate
Briefly, Mr. Hale is entitled to two main types of benefits under the RCMP Superannuation Act. One is his basic disability pension payable under that act which is related to salary and service. Other benefits are determined under the Pension Act and the Department of Veterans Affairs treatment regulations as if Mr. Hale were a veteran with disabilities attributable to military service.
It is my understanding that with Mr. Hale's release from the hospital on November 4, 1976, came the suspension of a portion of these other benefits. He is still, however, in receipt of certain basic benefits, and further, he will be entitled to a substantial increase in the attendance allowance which has been payable to him throughout his hospitalization and which will of necessity have to be increased by virtue of the care he will require at home.
The Canadian Pension Commission is presently examining Mr. Hale's situation and assessing the grade of attendance allowances under the Pension Act which would be payable to Mr. Hale under the RCMP Superannuation Act. Under these circumstances the minister will be in a position to reply fully on this matter within the next few days when all the departments together have assessed the situation fully, and I hope the answer which will be arrived at will satisfy the concern expressed by the hon. member this evening.
