subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBLE CHANGE IN LOCATION OF AIRBORNE REGIMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBLE CHANGE IN LOCATION OF AIRBORNE REGIMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise this evening because of the non-answer I received from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) to my question which is reported in Hansard for November 8, 1976, at page 835. My question had to do with the alleged reorganization of the Canadian Airborne Regiment now located in Edmonton, Alberta, and its proposed move to several separate locations in eastern Canada.
The reports from the media indicate that the future goal of reorganization and relocation of the Canadian Airborne Regiment remains uncertain, and it is also reported that a specific recommendation has been made by the Department of National Defence to the cabinet.
The implication of any major reorganization or relocation of the Canadian Airborne Regiment creates many significant implications, the most important of which are as follows: operational effectiveness, morale, training problems, relocation costs, and economic impact. Let us look at these items individually.
The Canadian Airborne Regiment as currently organized is a balanced combat-capable force comprising a balance of arms and services which are trained in parachute and air mobile operation giving the regiment a quick capability to reach any threatened area of the Canadian Arctic or any other location where its operational capability may be required. The Canadian Airborne Regiment parachute capability enables the regiment to be employed operationally in the Arctic without reliance on over-land or over-sea lines of communication. This

unique capability is the primary justification for the Canadian Airborne Regiment.
With regard to morale, constant uncertainty surrounding the future of the Canadian Airborne Regiment which has resulted from media leaks during the past year and a half has created and continues to create serious morale and motivation problems in the regiment. Because of its uncertain future it also appears that postings to the regiment have been restricted. Therefore the force has become seriously under strength. This combination of factors, in light of its previous top priority 100 per cent manning rationale, has seriously upset all ranks of the regiment at Edmonton.
With regard to training, since World War II, over 30 years ago, it has been the aim of military planners to concentrate all the components of an airborne force into a single location for the most economical, effective, and responsible training. These components include Canadian Airborne Regiment Hercules transport aircraft, an airborne training centre and a parachute packing and maintenance depot. After many studies and a great deal of analysis it was finally agreed in 1967 to concentrate all airborne elements at a single location in Edmonton. It is therefore only in the last few years that an effective training program has been achieved in Canada. To plan to dismember this Canadian airborne regiment concentration would appear to be foolhardy and expensive.
With respect to relocation costs, the present location in Edmonton includes a complete range of satisfactory hangars, training buildings, class rooms, offices, etc. for a complete airborne force. To move out of these highly satisfactory buildings and relocate elsewhere will undoubtedly involve enormous costs, probably exceeding $20 million. It must be borne in mind that to replace the current ideal situation would also require a comparable air base facility with runways, 24-hour flying capability, hangars, maintenance facilities and so forth.
Not only are the relocation costs in dollars but also in hardships for individuals who must buy new homes and place children in new schools, and for the working members of families to find new jobs if this is possible in a new location.
The CAR is the third largest employer of personnel in the city of Edmonton and the consequent loss of this very large and influential consumer force will cause serious distress to many merchants and businessmen in the Edmonton communities affected. To date there has been no satisfactory explanation, or indeed any explanation, given to explain the rationale behind the alleged proposal to re-organize and relocate the Canadian Airborne Regiment to some unknown destination in eastern Canada. It is only by a full and honest exposure of the reasons put forward by the department for such a move that an intelligent analysis and criticism of the implications can be made, and the answers better damn well be forthcoming.

speechtext:

November 18, 1976

refers to a non-answer he got from the minister. I do not see how anyone could term the minister's answer a non-answer. I shall quote briefly from it. He said:
I have not made a decision so far. I realize the uncertainty. All options are open and I want to remove that uncertainty as soon as possible. I do not want to shoot from the hip because 1 know many people arc concerned about the move.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I again raise the question of the possible establishment of a uranium refinery in the province of Saskatchewan. I may appear to be persistent in respect to this particular inquiry. Quite frankly the reason is that I have not received what I consider to be a reasonable answer. The parliamentary secretary is here and I am most concerned about obtaining this information because I do not want anyone to accuse either the minister or his parliamentary secretary of misleading the people of Saskatchewan. It is in this frame of mind that I raise the question again tonight. I know the parliamentary secretary would not want to be accused of misleading the people of Saskatchewan.
The fact of the matter is that when 1 asked the question on a previous occasion, as I did on November 16 during the question period, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) indicated that he was not prepared to reveal any information with regard to the establishment of this refinery near Saskatoon, or in any other part of Saskatchewan. Rather than reveal the nature of any agreement between the federal government and the government of Saskatchewan on this matter he keeps referring to Eldorado's press release relating to the establishment of a refinery.
It is fine for the minister to answer that way, but the press release does not give us any information about the plans of Eldorado about which I have been asking, time and time again. I say to the minister now that if he persists in this some people-not myself-will accuse him and his parliamentary
Adjournment Debate
secretary of misleading the people of Saskatchewan. If the parliamentary secretary does not want to be accused of misleading the people he should let us know details of the plans the government has in this area.
Let me read from the press release where the minister and the parliamentary secretary indicate they are giving full details of their plans in Saskatchewan. This is a four-page release dated July 21, and one paragraph referring to a refinery reads as follows:
A probable outlay of $50 million or more on a new uranium refinery. Eldorado now is actively considering a number of potential sites for a refinery that would employ 150, and begin production in the early 1980's. Detailed planning of this chemical plant awaits economic, engineering and environmental studies now in progress.
Another press release stated that a decision respecting the selection of a site would be made in a matter of weeks. Months have gone by, Mr. Speaker, and I have been unable to obtain any indication from the government of the sites being considered other than the one near Saskatoon. I have not been able to get any details of environmental studies carried out near Saskatoon or other areas, either. I say that in this case there is the appearance of a conspiracy of silence between the federal government, and the provincial government of Saskatchewan. The provincial government came under the most severe censure from its party membership at a provincial convention last week-end when its policy with respect to the establishment of the refinery was called into question.
I again ask the parliamentary secretary not to leave the impression that he or the minister is attempting to avoid answering this question. I ask him, in the spirit indicated in the Speech from the Throne of a new government approach of openness, to please give the details. We were led to believe that there would be full information available on government activities and that we would have participatory democracy.
In this situation it is most important that the people of the area have full opportunity to examine the facts and the alternatives, including the environmental studies, so that they can reach a meaningful decision based on facts rather than be apprehensive due to the silence of the government. I am receiving many inquiries on this issue, Mr. Speaker. I do not raise this from any selfish motive but because my constituents and the people of Saskatchewan would like to know what the government has in mind. I intend to continue raising this matter until such time as we get the answers.

Adjournment Debate
The hon. member suggested that perhaps the minister or the parliamentary secretary has been deceiving the population of Saskatchewan. I do not know about that; I have not been accused of that by others. The hon. member has so accused me, but I have not been accused by the people of Saskatchewan, as he has been. I am thinking, for instance, of the position of Mr. Messer. I wish that I did not have to repeat what I said previously. I said on November 8 that Jack Messer, the provincial minister of natural resources, said that the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) was trying to mislead the people of Saskatchewan and create a commotion over this matter.
I refer again to the press release issued on October 14 by Eldorado Nuclear Limited. Again I am forced to read some parts of the press release. It says on the first page:
Gordon Burton, director of corporate affairs for the company, said the purpose of the options is to allow Eldorado Nuclear to conduct detailed environmental and engineering studies of the site to determine whether it would be suitable for a refinery.
Let us not jump to conclusions. It seems that a decision has not been reached. I continue quoting from page 1 of the press release:
'It is emphasized that the company has not yet made a decision to proceed,' Mr. Burton said. This decision is dependent on many factors, not the least of which is the assurance of a supply of concentrates from proposed new mines in the northern part of the province.'
